options: Authentication — verifying who the user is
quiz.explain: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework, not an authentication protocol. Authentication is handled by OpenID Connect on top of OAuth.

quiz.q: In the hotel analogy, receiving the key to room 405 only (and not room 407) corresponds to what?
quiz.explain: Checking the booking ID and ID proof is authentication; getting restricted access to just your room is authorization.

quiz.q: Which comes first in the process?
options: They always happen at the same moment
Only one of them ever happens
quiz.explain: Identity is verified first (authentication), then restricted access is granted (authorization).

quiz.q: Ramesh signs up on Zomato with his Facebook account. Where does he type his Facebook password?
quiz.explain: The browser is redirected to Facebook's login page; the credentials go only to the provider, never to the client app.

quiz.q: After the user gives consent in the authorization code grant, what does the authorization server send to the client's redirect URI?
quiz.explain: An authorization code is sent via the redirect URI. The client then exchanges it for an access token in the backend.

quiz.q: What does Zomato's backend send to Facebook's token endpoint to get the access token?
options: Authorization code + client ID + client secret
The access token it already has
quiz.explain: The client exchanges the code together with its client ID and client secret, server-to-server, for an access token.

quiz.q: Why isn't the authorization code itself used as the access token?
options: It is too long to send in a header
It passes through the browser and can be seen, so the token is obtained in the backend with the client secret
The resource server cannot read codes
quiz.explain: Up to the redirect everything is in the browser, so the code is visible. The exchange needs the client secret and happens server-to-server.

quiz.q: Zomato calls Facebook's profile API with the access token. What does the resource server do before returning data?
options: Asks the authorization server to validate the token
Asks Ramesh to log in again
quiz.explain: The resource server checks the token with the authorization server; valid → profile details (only consented fields) returned, invalid → rejected.

quiz.q: In the Zomato + Facebook example, which OAuth actor is Zomato?
quiz.explain: Zomato is the client application requesting access on the user's behalf. Ramesh is the resource owner.

quiz.q: An access token expires after 1 hour. What lets the client get a new one without repeating the whole flow?
quiz.explain: A refresh token is long-lived; the client sends it to the token endpoint to obtain a new access token.

quiz.q: User 2 can read and edit a file but not delete it. Which OAuth concept expresses this?
quiz.explain: Scope is the set of permissions the client requests — the level of access within a resource.

quiz.q: Which grant type is used when a user signs in to a third-party app with their Google/Facebook/LinkedIn account?
quiz.explain: The authorization code grant covers sign-up/login to third-party apps via a provider account. Client credentials (mostly used for APIs) comes next session.

cards.back: **Open Authorization**. Version 2.0 is current; 1.0 was less secure and is no longer used.
An authorization framework that lets an application access a user's resources on another application on their behalf, without sharing credentials.
Authorization. Authentication is handled by **OpenID Connect**, though people commonly say "OAuth" for both.
Authentication verifies identity (who are you?); authorization grants restricted access (what can you access?). Authentication comes first.
The authentication (identity) layer on top of OAuth.
Resource owner, client, authorization server, resource server.
The user who owns the data/account being accessed (Ramesh in the example).
The application requesting access to protected resources on behalf of the user (Zomato).
Handles authentication/authorization and issues access tokens — e.g. Okta, Auth0 in companies.
Hosts the protected resources. For our MuleSoft APIs, the worker/runtime hosting the API.

cards.front: Explain the OAuth dance (authorization code grant)
cards.back: Login with provider → enter credentials on provider → consent → auth code to client's redirect URI → client exchanges code + client ID/secret for access token → calls resource server with token → token validated → data returned.

cards.front: Why isn't the auth code used as the access token?
cards.back: It passes through the browser and can be seen; the token is obtained in the backend using the code plus the client secret.

cards.front: Prerequisite for "Login with Facebook" on Zomato
cards.back: Zomato registered with Facebook's authorization server beforehand — it has a client ID/secret and a known redirect URI.
A temporary code the client receives after the user authorizes the request.
Token the client uses to call the resource server. Lifetime is configured — typically 1, 2 or 24 hours.
Long-lived token the client sends to the token endpoint to get a new access token when the current one expires.
The specific permissions the client requests — e.g. read only vs. read/write vs. read/write/delete.
The method by which the client obtains the access token. Examples: authorization code, client credentials, resource owner password.
The registered URI where the authorization server sends the user (and code) after authorization.
The authorization server endpoint that issues tokens.

cards.front: When is the authorization code grant used?
cards.back: When users sign up/log in to third-party apps with Google, Facebook, LinkedIn or another provider account.

cards.front: Why does Zomato get only GET profile access?
cards.back: Ramesh consented to share only a few details — no POST/PATCH/DELETE. That restricted access is authorization.

cards.front: Most-used grant type in the API field
cards.back: **Client credentials grant** (instructor's observation).
